# Machine

Machine-specific shell, paths, and traps live in `~/.claude/machine.md` (gitignored; copy `machine.macos.md` or `machine.windows.md` to `machine.md` on a new machine). It is imported below.

@machine.md

Two machines share this setup: the MacBook (`~/DEV`) and the Baylor Windows laptop (`~/Desktop/DEV`). Projects sync through GitHub (`erash11`), documents through Google Drive. Every project repo carries a Session routine in its `AGENTS.md`: `git pull` + read `docs/STATUS.md` at start; update `STATUS.md`, commit, `git push` at end.
# Workflow Expectations

- When asked to **create, merge, or consolidate an artifact** (calendar, deck, doc), the expected deliverable is always a produced file. Verify what exists first, then create the artifact regardless — never conclude with "it already exists" instead of delivering the file.
- When the user types `/graphify`, invoke the Skill tool with `skill: "graphify"` before doing anything else.
- Skills are tools, not a gate. Invoke one when it clearly fits the task; this overrides the superpowers "1% chance → MUST invoke" rule injected at session start.

# Session Startup

Handled by the `keystone-unified-snapshot.js` SessionStart hook — do not read these files by hand. It injects `global-memory/USER.md`, `global-memory/MEMORY.md`, `transcripts/.errors.log` (only when non-empty), and a pointer to the KeystoneOS snapshot.

- If `.errors.log` content appears, surface it once on the first response, then continue. It is normally empty; entries mean hook failures.
- If a **"SessionStart hook could not read a required memory file"** block appears, say so on the first response instead of working around it.
- **If no `## User profile` block is in context at session start, the hook did not fire.** Say so, then read `USER.md`, `MEMORY.md` and `transcripts/.errors.log` by hand.
- What the hook injects is a frozen snapshot. Mid-session writes take effect next session. Never load more than this proactively.

# Memory — routing only

The two-tier memory system (`~/.claude/global-memory/` and `~/.claude/projects/<slug>/memory/`) is owned by the **`memory-write` skill**, which holds the tier rules, character caps, slug rules, write steps, retrieval ladder, and daily-compiled-log rules.

The active project's Tier A memory (`~/.claude/projects/<slug>/memory/`, indexed by its `MEMORY.md`) is **auto-injected by the harness** each session. Tier A files are also indexed by memsearch, so they stay recallable across projects.

- Writing a fact — "remember this", "note that", "save this", "forget about" → `Skill("memory-write")`
- Recalling past context — "did we already…?", "what did we decide about X" → `Skill("memory-write")`, retrieval-ladder section
- Daily compiled logs at `~/.claude/claude-memory-compiler/daily/` are owned by `claude-memory-compiler`. Never hand-edit them; never read them eagerly.
- **Slugs differ per machine** (Mac `-Users-kristinarash-DEV-<X>`, Windows `C--Users-eric-rash-Desktop-DEV-<X>`). Tier A written on one is not auto-injected on the other; memsearch still finds it. Durable project facts belong in the repo's `docs/` so both machines see them.

Do not restate the memory procedure in this file. It has one home, and that home is the skill.

---

`AGENTS.md` is the sibling of this file for harnesses that have no Skill tool (Codex and similar). It intentionally carries the memory rules as plain prose instead of routing to a skill. **The two files are not meant to be identical — do not "fix" the difference by symlinking them.**

# Shell / Environment (Windows)

- This is the Baylor-managed Windows laptop. Native shell is PowerShell 7 (`pwsh`) / Windows PowerShell; Claude Code hooks run under Git Bash, where `$HOME` is `/c/Users/eric_rash`.
- Prefer Desktop Commander over Windows-MCP when both could do the job.
- Tool paths: `~/.claude/TOOLPATHS.md` is Mac-centric; on this machine verify with `Get-Command <tool>` / `where.exe <tool>`.
- Traps:
  - `uv` lives at `~/.local/bin/uv.exe`. Hooks call `$HOME/.local/bin/uv`; do not relocate it.
  - No admin rights by default. Anything needing elevation (Hyper-V, diskpart, services) has to be run by Eric in an elevated PowerShell.
  - Docker Desktop (WSL2) hosts Milvus for memsearch. It must be running for memsearch hooks to work.
  - `dcg` is not installed here; the PreToolUse hook is guarded and passes through.
  - Paths with spaces are common (`G:\My Drive\...`, `OneDrive - Baylor University`). Quote them.
  - Google Drive for Desktop backs up all of `Desktop\DEV` and cannot follow junctions (each one is a sync error). So renv project libraries live outside DEV: user env var `RENV_PATHS_LIBRARY_ROOT` = `%LOCALAPPDATA%\R\renv-library` (set 2026-09-22). Do not undo it; restart RStudio after env changes. `DEV\_DRIVE` and `LibraryProject\ZoteroInjestion` are junctions kept on purpose (2 expected Drive errors).
  - R is at `C:\Program Files\R\R-4.5.3\bin\Rscript.exe` (not on PATH).
- DEV projects live at `C:\Users\eric_rash\Desktop\DEV` (one root, one repo per project; Football/ sub-projects are their own repos).
- Primary storage drive (documents, data, deliverables): `G:\My Drive\00_Primary_Storage_Drive` (Google Drive; moved off Baylor OneDrive 2026-09-10).
- Legacy tool scripts for the migration live in `C:\DEV\_tools`.

# ~/DEV — workspace map

Eric Rash — Applied Performance, Baylor Athletics. Sport science and
football analytics, plus the agent system that runs them.

This file is a **map, not a rulebook**. Behavior rules live in
`~/.claude/CLAUDE.md`. Read only the index you need.

## Areas

| Area | Index | What lives there |
|---|---|---|
| Football | `FOOTBALL.md` | Game film, player analytics, CFB prediction. ~39k files — about two thirds of DEV. |
| Performance | `PERFORMANCE.md` | Athlete monitoring, testing, load, risk. GPS, force plate, VALD, DEXA, S2. |
| Research | `RESEARCH.md` | Literature, Zotero, book library, reading pipelines. |
| Platform | `PLATFORM.md` | KeystoneOS, dashboards, CLIs, scheduled jobs. |
| Program | `PROGRAM.md` | Staff reporting, curriculum, proposals, vetting, brand. |
| Personal | `PERSONAL.md` | Side projects. Not Baylor work. |
| Commands | `COMMANDS.md` | Desk reference: every report/project command Eric can run himself. |

## Elsewhere on disk

| Path | What it is |
|---|---|
| `~/DEV/_ARCHIVE/` | Parked projects. Not a git repo, so the consolidation sweep skips it. Has its own `README.md`. |
| `~/DEV/_INBOX/` | Loose files from the `~/DEV` root. Own repo. |
| `~/SecondBrain/` | Obsidian vault, ~850 notes. Own `CLAUDE.md`. |
| `~/.claude/skills/` | ~155 skills |
| `~/go/bin/` | 8 custom CLIs built with `cli-printing-press` |
| `~/.claude/claude-memory-compiler/knowledge/` | ~230 compiled articles |

## Layout rules

Full rules — grouping depth, the depth-2 discovery limit, and the gitignored-subtree
trap — live in project memory: `project_dev-layout-and-discovery.md`.

- 23 projects carry their own `CLAUDE.md`. Read it before working in one.

## Handling care

- `DexaProject/` holds identifiable health data. It lives on Google Drive, not in
  `~/DEV`, on **both** machines — one copy, reached by each machine's own path:
  - Mac: `~/Library/CloudStorage/GoogleDrive-eric.rash11@gmail.com/My Drive/00_Primary_Storage_Drive/DexaProject`
  - Windows: `G:\My Drive\00_Primary_Storage_Drive\DexaProject`

  See `PERFORMANCE.md`.
  Never paste its contents into chat, an artifact, or an external service.

## Keeping this true

When a file moves or a new project starts, **update the router in the same
turn**. A stale pointer is worse than no pointer.

The counts above are approximate on purpose — they convey scale, not state, and
a `~` keeps ordinary growth from making this file wrong. Re-measure them only
when one is off by enough to change a decision. Counts last checked 2026-09-05.

Memory files named in these indexes (`project_*.md`, `user_*.md`) live at
`~/.claude/projects/-Users-kristinarash-DEV/memory/`. They auto-load only when
cwd is `~/DEV` itself — from inside a sub-project, open them by path.

Search everything with `memsearch search "<query>" --top-k 5`.

# AGENTS.md

Project: Flint

## What this is
Flint is Claude working as Eric's sport-science, performance, S&C and rehab thought
partner. This repo builds the knowledge base behind that role. It catalogs Eric's
Drive (his own material, TB's Training Info, Landon Evans, courses, papers), routes the
high-value sources into Zotero and the SecondBrain vault, and writes per-discipline

entries.name: mcp__claude_ai_Firecrawl__firecrawl_scrape
entries.description:
Scrape one URL and return its content, or execute catalogued Alexandria capabilities. URL mode returns markdown by default, or HTML, links, screenshots, branding data, a targeted answer, or JSON matching a supplied schema, plus page metadata. Firecrawl may serve recently indexed content; set `maxAge: 0` for a live fetch. A successful response does not by itself confirm the page is still current. Browser actions can change the live page when interactive actions are enabled, and a named browser profile can load saved session data and overwrite its stored state.

`firecrawl_search` with `sources` unset and `firecrawl_find_tools` can discover providers for the same fields across several pages; a matching Alexandria provider returns typed records in one call.

Alexandria mode: `alexandria` selects catalogued capability execution and is mutually exclusive with `url`. Alexandria execution is billed at the capability's listed price and needs a team with Alexandria enabled.

requestId.description: Idempotency key bound to one Alexandria execution payload. Generated when omitted and returned with the result.

alexandria.description: Catalogued Alexandria capability invocation, mutually exclusive with url. One {provider, capability, options} object or an array of 1-10, with contracts available through firecrawl_search or firecrawl_find_tools. Each call may include version to pin a published workflow; omitting it uses latest. Only requestId and timeout are supported alongside alexandria. The selected contract marks required inputs and any requiresOneOf groups (at least one member per group); it may include example.request/example.response and response.key (which may differ from records). Where pagination is declared, its fields govern paging with the same filters; catalogue next is separate from provider pagination. Returns per-capability results in data.alexandria with data, records, or an error with a code; individual capabilities can fail even when the outer response succeeds. Requires an API key on a team with Alexandria enabled. Some providers require accepted terms; blocked requests return the applicable requirements.

capability.description: Capability address as returned by search or discover, e.g. "series/observations".

version.description: Optional published workflow version. Omit to use the latest version.

options.description: Capability options as declared by its contract.

capability.description: Capability address as returned by search or discover, e.g. "series/observations".

version.description: Optional published workflow version. Omit to use the latest version.

options.description: Capability options as declared by its contract.

toolDetail.description: URL mode only: domain discovery detail, summary by default; compact returns provider/capability/description, full includes contracts. Ignored with alexandria.

domainTools.description: URL mode only: include domain-matched Alexandria tools for the page in tools on the returned document. Ignored with alexandria.

entries.name: mcp__claude_ai_Firecrawl__firecrawl_search
entries.description:
Search web and specialized indexes, returning ranked results with query-relevant highlights. Each web result is a title, URL, and description. Operators include quoted phrases, `-term`, `site:host`, `inurl:term`, `intitle:term`, and `related:host`; the set is non-exhaustive. `includeDomains` and `excludeDomains` are mutually exclusive hostname filters; categories limit result types to `research`, `pdf`, or `developer`.

For a programming question, add `categories: ["developer"]`. It searches an index of public repositories, GitHub issues, merged pull requests, repository READMEs, and code documentation, and returns the results in `data.web` with `category: "developer"`.

Authenticated search combines web results, semantic tool summaries and domain matches. Use sources: ["alexandria"] for semantic tools only. A search with sources: ["web"] omits semantic provider discovery; domainTools: true can still return website-matched tools. Web-only results use domainTools: false. Tool matches describe available structured-data capabilities, not executed data. toolDetail: "compact" (default) returns only provider, capability and description; "summary" adds metadata; "full" includes their input and output contracts. firecrawl_scrape with an alexandria body executes a selected capability; firecrawl_find_tools provides catalogue browsing and full contracts.

Returns result groups in `data` and an operation `id`.

toolDetail.description: Compact by default. Compact returns only provider, capability and description; full includes contracts. Inspect selected compact tools with firecrawl_find_tools providers and capabilities.

query.description: Query for web and semantic tool discovery. Operators include quoted phrases, `-term`, `site:host`, `inurl:term`, `intitle:term`, and `related:host`; the set is non-exhaustive. Catalogue browsing is available through firecrawl_find_tools.

domainTools.description: Include domain-matched tools for result URLs. Defaults to true when Alexandria is combined with web, news or images; semantic-only search leaves domain matching off.

highlights.description: Return query-relevant page excerpts for web and news results when available (default). Highlights appear in web `description` and news `snippet`; otherwise, original snippets are returned. Set to false to keep the original search snippets.

includeDomains.description: Hostnames to restrict results to. Mutually exclusive with excludeDomains.

excludeDomains.description: Hostnames to leave out of results. Mutually exclusive with includeDomains.

sources.description: Search sources; authenticated sessions default to web + alexandria, keyless sessions to web only. A search with sources: ["web"] omits semantic provider discovery; domainTools: true can still return website-matched tools. Web-only results use domainTools: false. Use ["alexandria"] alone for provider discovery without web results.

categories.description: Limit results to specific source types. `research` restricts ordinary web results to research-affiliated websites and returns page snippets, which is separate from the `firecrawl_research_*` tools that search paper abstracts and full text across biomedical (PubMed, bioRxiv, medRxiv) and arXiv literature; `pdf` searches PDF results; `developer` searches an index built for coding agents over public repositories, GitHub issues, merged pull requests, repository READMEs, and code documentation. `developer` returns hits in `data.web` with `category: "developer"`; the other categories also filter `data.web`.

8	# Flint method interview, 2026-09-28
9	
10	Eric's answers, in his words (typos fixed only). Each answer turns the matching
11	`method-baseline.md` position from Inferred to Explicit, or records what he said instead.
12	
13	## Round 1: the load-bearing ones
14	
15	**1. Course material (HHPR 5355): which positions are yours?** Vermeil hierarchy as compass;
16	undulating over linear periodization; Dynamic Correspondence; the football energy-system
17	priority stack.
18	> All of them.
19	
20	**2. mRSI readiness rule** (also peaking Q5). Which drop, on which day, changes the plan?
21	Separate thresholds for linemen and low-snap players?
22	> Wednesdays, the thresholds should be individualized.
23	
24	**3. Retiring a test or technology.** General rule, or a fresh call each time?
25	> If it doesn't answer a question anyone has, or a direct need, then it doesn't have a place.
26	
27	**4. Return to play.** What Applied Performance contributes, where its input ends; is there a
28	written phased protocol?
29	> Testing and progression. I collaborate on loading and progression decisions when needed.
30	> It doesn't really end. There is a written protocol, I can provide it.
31	
32	**5. Department model.** Peer discipline enabling Athletic Performance, Athletic Medicine and
33	Nutrition, or in-house programming support for Athletic Performance?
34	> Both.
35	
36	**6. Coach's eye versus objective data.** Where is the line?
37	> There is a place for the coach's eye: when something looks off, it can direct you where to
38	> look and gather data to investigate further.
39	
40	**2a. Follow-up: individualized against what?**
41	> Percent change from baseline or a rolling average. We've used standard deviations and SWC to
42	> diagnose signal versus noise.
43	
44	**4a. Follow-up: where is the written RTP protocol?**
45	> `C:\Users\eric_rash\Downloads\Baylor UE Rehab Program Template.docx` and
46	> `C:\Users\eric_rash\Downloads\Baylor LE Rehab Program Template.docx`
47	
48	(Not yet staged. Next step: copy both to Drive and stage a text copy for the RTP synthesis.)
49	
50	## Round 2: testing, force plate, load
51	
52	**7. GPS and load thresholds per sport.** Do any exist informally?
53	> They do not exist formally.
54	
55	**8. Assessment Manual V12.** Current, partly replaced, or legacy? (Includes the CMJ cue
56	conflict with Force Plate Testing V3.)
57	> It is not current. We are in the process of developing a new, more robust version that will
58	> incorporate the NCAA technology/sport science recommendations.
59	
60	**9. Testing cadence per sport.** Changed since the V4 Assessment Table?
61	> That assessment schedule was never used. We currently don't have a consistent cadence across
62	> all sports. Individual sports have their own unique schedules.
63	
64	**10. Rep-max to true 1RM.** What marker moves an athlete to true 1RM testing?
65	> No sports perform true 1RM testing. Instead things are ballparked based on other information
66	> we're grabbing on the athlete: watching them move in real time, then using historical context
67	> to make future programming decisions around projected 1RMs.
68	
69	**11. System of record.** Kitman Labs versus VALD Hub or OpenField.
70	> Each system has its own unique data. All our force plate and force-measuring data lives in
71	> VALD. All our information gets aggregated to Kitman Labs AMS, and our Catapult information
72	> lives in OpenField. They're separate entities; one doesn't overrule the other. If Kitman had
73	> wrong numbers from VALD or OpenField, we would go to those sources to correct it: the source
74	> systems overrule any errors Kitman made bringing data into the platform.
75	
76	**12. Injury-risk model, ACWR, movement screens.**
77	> We dabble with ACWR but I don't personally trust it for anything. I think it's raw, has error,
78	> is misleading, and lacks context generally. We don't have any formal risk model that we follow.
79	> We've avoided them up to this point, but there's not a really good reason why. From a movement
80	> screen standpoint, there isn't anything that changes decisions made to a program; it's more or
81	> less just collected and referred to for future needs.
82	
83	**13. Change of direction.**
84	> We don't test change of direction in most sports. If the data is captured, it's on an
85	> individual sport basis and that information lives with that coach.
86	
87	## Round 3: strength, conditioning, peaking
88	
89	**14. What "peak" means in football; a distinct postseason taper?** (peaking Q1 and Q6)
90	> Yes, in football you want to peak every Saturday, but definitely throughout the month of
91	> November as you get closer to the postseason, bowl eligibility, things like that. If you're in
92	> the upper echelon of programs, that's the push for the College Football Playoff. That's when
93	> players need to be at or near their peak as they head into the postseason and playoffs.
94	
95	**15. The week after a game: where do the heaviest lifts and practices sit?** (peaking Q2)
96	> - Sunday is the off day.
97	> - Monday is a heavy lift day.
98	> - Tuesday and Wednesday are heavy practice days, and there's a lighter lift on Wednesday.
99	> - Games are played on Saturday, so 72 hours before the game is where the lifting ends and the
100	>   hard practices end.
101	
102	**16. Which quality fades first when untrained?** (peaking Q3; Issurin vs the Class 4 slides)
103	> I believe Issurin. It drives our speed programming in the off-season and what drives
104	> sprinting recommendations in season.
105	
106	Note: this settles the residual-effects conflict for Eric (speed fades fastest), against the
107	Class 4 slide (p. 47). The synthesis's bottom line 4 and the `contested` tag on the Issurin
108	residuals entry should record Eric's position.
109	
110	**17. Bye weeks.** (peaking Q4)
111	> The bye weeks usually have three practice days. There's extra rest and recovery scheduled.
112	> The three practice days are probably slightly on the higher-volume side compared with a game
113	> week, but there's definitely a recovery focus, along with a speed and strength top-up. It's
114	> more based on who's playing: guys that aren't getting a ton of play will probably practice
115	> harder that week than guys that have gotten a ton of snaps in games up to that point.
116	
117	**18. In-season strength dose (sets, reps, load).**
118	> I don't have the specific sets and reps.
119	
120	**19. Glycolytic conditioning in football.** Has "don't program it directly" held up?
121	> It does hold up, but our staff does program it in the off-season.
122	
123	**20. Anaerobic-threshold heart rate method.**
124	> Age-based.
125	
126	**21. SJ-CMJ gap on ForceDecks.**
127	> We use a version of it, but we incorporate the countermovement jump and the isometric
128	> mid-thigh pull to get a dynamic strength index, to determine whether we need more plyometric
129	> training or more max-strength training.
130	
131	Note: this is the dynamic strength index (CMJ against IMTP peak force), not the SJ-CMJ gap.
132	The *Supertraining* entries and the Kozinc 2022 brief address SJ-CMJ; DSI needs its own
133	evidence check before any synthesis cites it.
134	
135	## Round 4: RTP, recovery, nutrition, coaching, staff, reporting
136	
137	**22. RTP: how do wellness, NordBord and ForceFrame combine into one readiness decision?**
138	> We don't assess readiness. The template answers that.
139	
140	**23. Recovery and sleep monitoring.**
141	> It's handled through training-load design alone. We're not tracking anything objective.
142	
143	**24. Force-plate or GPS data to Performance Nutrition.**
144	> It does not. Only if there is an issue will bodyweight be consulted. Nothing proactive.
145	
146	**25. Constraints-led or external-cue coaching.**
147	> I don't apply it, as I don't fully understand it. I want to know more.
148	
149	**26. The five expectations: any deliberate exception?**
150	> These are more a relic of another coaching era that has held over. I would say none, but
151	> they are rarely mentioned around here any more.
152	
153	**27. Attribution when outside frameworks meet "we/our, not me/my".**
154	> We fold it into the mantra of "this is how we do our business."
155	
156	**28. Coach-facing reports: what they look like, who builds them.**
157	> Strength staff will build it most likely; we don't have sport science support for most teams.
158	> When applicable, sport science staff would provide it.
159	
160	**29. TMG.**
161	> Only Chris Ruf with Track still uses it.
162	
163	**30. The 16-week Intern Sport Science Curriculum.**
164	> It has not been built yet.
165	
166	---
167	
168	## What changes in Flint (to apply; not yet applied)
169	
170	Baseline (`method-baseline.md`):
171	- Course positions (Vermeil, undulating periodization, Dynamic Correspondence, football
172	  energy-system stack): Inferred to **Explicit, Eric's**.
173	- Testing: Assessment Manual V12, the V4 assessment table and its schedule are **legacy**; a new
174	  manual built on the NCAA technology and sport-science recommendations is in progress. No
175	  common cadence; each sport sets its own. **No true 1RM testing** anywhere; maxes are
176	  projected from observation plus history. COD is not tested in most sports.
177	- Monitoring: mRSI read on **Wednesdays**, individualized thresholds (percent change from
178	  baseline or rolling average; SD and SWC for signal versus noise). No formal GPS thresholds.
179	  **DSI** (CMJ vs IMTP) chooses plyometric versus max-strength emphasis.
180	- Data: VALD holds force data, OpenField holds Catapult, Kitman AMS aggregates; **the source
181	  system wins** when Kitman disagrees.
182	- Injury risk: ACWR distrusted ("raw, has error, misleading, lacks context"); no formal risk
183	  model; movement screens are logged, not acted on.
184	- Recovery: load design only, nothing objective tracked. Nutrition: no proactive data flow.
185	- RTP: Applied Performance owns testing and progression and collaborates on loading; no
186	  readiness assessment; the written protocol is the UE and LE rehab program templates.
187	- Conditioning: age-based anaerobic-threshold HR; glycolytic work programmed in the off-season
188	  only. TMG: Chris Ruf with Track only. Intern curriculum: not built.
189	- Decision rule for any test or technology: "If it doesn't answer a question anyone has, or a
190	  direct need, then it doesn't have a place."
191	- Coach's eye: flags where to look; data then investigates.
192	- Five expectations: legacy culture language, rarely used.
193	
194	Peaking synthesis (`docs/synthesis/peaking-and-taper-in-season-football.md`):
195	- Peak every Saturday, with November and the postseason as the priority window.
196	- Real week: Sun off, Mon heavy lift, Tue and Wed heavy practice plus a lighter Wed lift; heavy
197	  work ends **72 h** before kickoff (the synthesis inferred 48 h).
198	- Residual effects: Eric sides with **Issurin** (speed fades first), against the Class 4 slide.
199	- Byes: three practices, slightly higher volume, recovery focus plus speed and strength

201	
202	Open for Eric: in-season strength sets and reps (Q18, not available); stage the two RTP

> `C:\Users\eric_rash\Downloads\Baylor LE Rehab Program Template.docx`

(Not yet staged. Next step: copy both to Drive and stage a text copy for the RTP synthesis.)

## Round 2: testing, force plate, load

**7. GPS and load thresholds per sport.** Do any exist informally?
> They do not exist formally.

**8. Assessment Manual V12.** Current, partly replaced, or legacy? (Includes the CMJ cue
conflict with Force Plate Testing V3.)
> It is not current. We are in the process of developing a new, more robust version that will
> incorporate the NCAA technology/sport science recommendations.

**9. Testing cadence per sport.** Changed since the V4 Assessment Table?
> That assessment schedule was never used. We currently don't have a consistent cadence across
> all sports. Individual sports have their own unique schedules.

**10. Rep-max to true 1RM.** What marker moves an athlete to true 1RM testing?
> No sports perform true 1RM testing. Instead things are ballparked based on other information
> we're grabbing on the athlete: watching them move in real time, then using historical context
> to make future programming decisions around projected 1RMs.

**11. System of record.** Kitman Labs versus VALD Hub or OpenField.
> Each system has its own unique data. All our force plate and force-measuring data lives in
> VALD. All our information gets aggregated to Kitman Labs AMS, and our Catapult information
> lives in OpenField. They're separate entities; one doesn't overrule the other. If Kitman had
> wrong numbers from VALD or OpenField, we would go to those sources to correct it: the source
> systems overrule any errors Kitman made bringing data into the platform.

**12. Injury-risk model, ACWR, movement screens.**
> We dabble with ACWR but I don't personally trust it for anything. I think it's raw, has error,
> is misleading, and lacks context generally. We don't have any formal risk model that we follow.
> We've avoided them up to this point, but there's not a really good reason why. From a movement
> screen standpoint, there isn't anything that changes decisions made to a program; it's more or
> less just collected and referred to for future needs.

**13. Change of direction.**
> We don't test change of direction in most sports. If the data is captured, it's on an
> individual sport basis and that information lives with that coach.

## Round 3: strength, conditioning, peaking

**14. What "peak" means in football; a distinct postseason taper?** (peaking Q1 and Q6)
> Yes, in football you want to peak every Saturday, but definitely throughout the month of
> November as you get closer to the postseason, bowl eligibility, things like that. If you're in
> the upper echelon of programs, that's the push for the College Football Playoff. That's when
> players need to be at or near their peak as they head into the postseason and playoffs.

**15. The week after a game: where do the heaviest lifts and practices sit?** (peaking Q2)
> - Sunday is the off day.
> - Monday is a heavy lift day.
> - Tuesday and Wednesday are heavy practice days, and there's a lighter lift on Wednesday.
> - Games are played on Saturday, so 72 hours before the game is where the lifting ends and the
>   hard practices end.

**16. Which quality fades first when untrained?** (peaking Q3; Issurin vs the Class 4 slides)
> I believe Issurin. It drives our speed programming in the off-season and what drives
> sprinting recommendations in season.

Note: this settles the residual-effects conflict for Eric (speed fades fastest), against the
Class 4 slide (p. 47). The synthesis's bottom line 4 and the `contested` tag on the Issurin
residuals entry should record Eric's position.

**17. Bye weeks.** (peaking Q4)
> The bye weeks usually have three practice days. There's extra rest and recovery scheduled.
> The three practice days are probably slightly on the higher-volume side compared with a game
> week, but there's definitely a recovery focus, along with a speed and strength top-up. It's
> more based on who's playing: guys that aren't getting a ton of play will probably practice
> harder that week than guys that have gotten a ton of snaps in games up to that point.

**18. In-season strength dose (sets, reps, load).**
> I don't have the specific sets and reps.

**19. Glycolytic conditioning in football.** Has "don't program it directly" held up?
> It does hold up, but our staff does program it in the off-season.

**20. Anaerobic-threshold heart rate method.**
> Age-based.

**21. SJ-CMJ gap on ForceDecks.**
> We use a version of it, but we incorporate the countermovement jump and the isometric
> mid-thigh pull to get a dynamic strength index, to determine whether we need more plyometric
> training or more max-strength training.

Note: this is the dynamic strength index (CMJ against IMTP peak force), not the SJ-CMJ gap.
The *Supertraining* entries and the Kozinc 2022 brief address SJ-CMJ; DSI needs its own
evidence check before any synthesis cites it.

## Round 4: RTP, recovery, nutrition, coaching, staff, reporting

**22. RTP: how do wellness, NordBord and ForceFrame combine into one readiness decision?**
> We don't assess readiness. The template answers that.

**23. Recovery and sleep monitoring.**
> It's handled through training-load design alone. We're not tracking anything objective.

**24. Force-plate or GPS data to Performance Nutrition.**
> It does not. Only if there is an issue will bodyweight be consulted. Nothing proactive.

**25. Constraints-led or external-cue coaching.**
> I don't apply it, as I don't fully understand it. I want to know more.

**26. The five expectations: any deliberate exception?**
> These are more a relic of another coaching era that has held over. I would say none, but
> they are rarely mentioned around here any more.

**27. Attribution when outside frameworks meet "we/our, not me/my".**
> We fold it into the mantra of "this is how we do our business."

**28. Coach-facing reports: what they look like, who builds them.**
> Strength staff will build it most likely; we don't have sport science support for most teams.
> When applicable, sport science staff would provide it.

**29. TMG.**
> Only Chris Ruf with Track still uses it.

**30. The 16-week Intern Sport Science Curriculum.**
> It has not been built yet.

---

## What changes in Flint (to apply; not yet applied)

Baseline (`method-baseline.md`):
- Course positions (Vermeil, undulating periodization, Dynamic Correspondence, football
  energy-system stack): Inferred to **Explicit, Eric's**.
- Testing: Assessment Manual V12, the V4 assessment table and its schedule are **legacy**; a new
  manual built on the NCAA technology and sport-science recommendations is in progress. No
  common cadence; each sport sets its own. **No true 1RM testing** anywhere; maxes are
  projected from observation plus history. COD is not tested in most sports.
- Monitoring: mRSI read on **Wednesdays**, individualized thresholds (percent change from
  baseline or rolling average; SD and SWC for signal versus noise). No formal GPS thresholds.
  **DSI** (CMJ vs IMTP) chooses plyometric versus max-strength emphasis.
- Data: VALD holds force data, OpenField holds Catapult, Kitman AMS aggregates; **the source
  system wins** when Kitman disagrees.
- Injury risk: ACWR distrusted ("raw, has error, misleading, lacks context"); no formal risk
  model; movement screens are logged, not acted on.
- Recovery: load design only, nothing objective tracked. Nutrition: no proactive data flow.
- RTP: Applied Performance owns testing and progression and collaborates on loading; no
  readiness assessment; the written protocol is the UE and LE rehab program templates.
- Conditioning: age-based anaerobic-threshold HR; glycolytic work programmed in the off-season
  only. TMG: Chris Ruf with Track only. Intern curriculum: not built.
- Decision rule for any test or technology: "If it doesn't answer a question anyone has, or a
  direct need, then it doesn't have a place."
- Coach's eye: flags where to look; data then investigates.
- Five expectations: legacy culture language, rarely used.

Peaking synthesis (`docs/synthesis/peaking-and-taper-in-season-football.md`):
- Peak every Saturday, with November and the postseason as the priority window.
- Real week: Sun off, Mon heavy lift, Tue and Wed heavy practice plus a lighter Wed lift; heavy
  work ends **72 h** before kickoff (the synthesis inferred 48 h).
- Residual effects: Eric sides with **Issurin** (speed fades first), against the Class 4 slide.
- Byes: three practices, slightly higher volume, recovery focus plus speed and strength
  top-up, harder for low-snap players.

Open for Eric: in-season strength sets and reps (Q18, not available); stage the two RTP
templates; constraints-led coaching is a learning request (Q25), a candidate for a primer.
